extracted.intended_audience: comic creators, First Amendment advocates, and members of the public interested in censorship and legal history
extracted.subtask_description: A concise historical and legal summary of the People v. Bruce obscenity prosecution, describing the statutory language relied on, the factual posture, the types of evidence and expert testimony presented, and the court's findings about obscenity and social value. Useful for readers wanting to understand how obscenity standards were applied to stand-up comedy and satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: New York Penal Code 1140 (statutory prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted statutory language barring certain performances: New York Penal Code 1140 barred “obscene, indecent, immoral, and impure dram, play, exhibition, and entertainment . . . which would tend to the corruption of the morals of youth and others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis the prosecution used to indict Bruce. The article presents the statute verbatim as the legal prohibition under which performances could be judged and prosecuted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's obscenity findings (three-part basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court concluded Bruce’s act “appealed to prurient interest,” was “patently offensive to the average person in the community,” and lacked “redeeming social importance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three articulated findings were the court’s basis for convicting Bruce; they map onto core elements courts have used to evaluate obscenity claims (prurience, offensiveness under community standards, and absence of redeeming social/artistic value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community standards (local offense test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the performance was “patently offensive to the average person in the community” — i.e., measured against local community standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense presented New York media experts who testified the performance did not offend local community standards; the prosecution countered with witnesses claiming it offended community morals. The page highlights community standards as a contested axis of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prurient interest / sexual arousal evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the performance “appealed to prurient interest” or was sexually arousing to an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense psychiatrists testified that Bruce’s performance was not sexually arousing; the prosecution sought to show it appealed to prurient interest. The article uses this to show that factual findings about sexual arousal were central to the obscenity determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redeeming social importance / artistic/social value
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work possesses social importance, literary/artistic merit, or other redeeming social value that would counter an obscenity finding (the court here found Bruce’s act lacked such redeeming social importance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense produced literary and art critics, and a petition from prominent cultural figures (Ginsberg, Dylan, Newman, etc.), to demonstrate social importance and artistic value. The presence or absence of such value was decisive in the court's assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and accuracy of eyewitness/investigator accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy and fidelity of undercover investigators’ notes and testimony about the performance (the article reports investigators read from hand-written notes that ‘butchered’ Bruce’s material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece emphasizes that prosecutors relied on accounts from undercover investigators whose handwritten notes reportedly misrepresented timing and delivery; Bruce lamented being judged by ‘his bad timing, his ego, his garbled language.’ This raises a criterion about whether evidence accurately captures performance context and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and weight of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of expert witnesses (sociologists, professors, literary/art critics, psychiatrists, media experts) to opine on decency, community impact, sexual arousal, and artistic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prosecution and defense both presented expert testimony: prosecution offered sociologists and literary experts to argue lack of merit and community harm; defense offered psychiatrists, media experts, and critics to rebut sexual-arousal and community-offense claims. The article treats the availability, credibility, and content of expert testimony as a key factor in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial tactics and evidence-gathering (undercover attendance, grand jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures by which the state assembled charges — sending undercover investigators to performances, relying on their reports, and presenting evidence to a grand jury to obtain an indictment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces a pattern of arrests across jurisdictions and highlights that NYC prosecutors used undercover attendance at Café Au Go Go shows to compile evidence leading to a grand jury indictment. This indicates that how evidence is collected (undercover observers, selections of shows/dates) is relevant to evaluating prosecutions for alleged obscenity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness and subjectivity of obscenity standards (risk of censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article asserts that vague ‘obscenity’ standards and subjective notions like ‘redeeming social importance’ and ‘community standards’ can be used to censor satirical speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBLDF’s commentary frames this as a normative criterion: laws and standards that are vague or subjectively applied pose risks to satire and comic expression. The piece uses Bruce’s case to illustrate how subjective standards can lead to suppression of socially important satire.
